source: Clark, Tafjord, Richardson (2020) Transformers as Soft Reasoners over Language (RuleTaker)
finding: A fine-tuned RoBERTa answers true/false questions over synthetic rule bases under a closed-world assumption, where unprovable means false (negation as failure). The rules include Sergot's 'birds' puzzle, a McCarthy-style default with an abnormality predicate.
numbers: About 99% accuracy on in-distribution depth-limited sets. On the hand-written Birds rulebase, zero-shot, all trained models except the no-reasoning baseline scored almost perfectly; the strongest model got one question wrong on Birds1. Removing a critical context sentence: 81.2% accuracy vs 99.4% on originals.
quote: our model's treatment of negation as failure (NAF) sometimes clashes with intuitions about NLI
limits: Closed-world negation as failure is a restricted non-monotonic semantics, not full default logic. Synthetic English. The authors note a clash: given only 'If my car does not have gas then it is not working', the model concludes 'not working' because it cannot prove 'has gas'.
agent_relevance: A transformer can follow 'normal unless abnormal' rules stated in the prompt. Silence-as-false must be marked explicitly in any lesson store, or the agent will treat missing evidence as a negative fact.

source: Tafjord, Dalvi Mishra, Clark (2021) ProofWriter: Generating Implications, Proofs, and Abductive Statements over Natural Language
finding: T5-11B generates implications and proofs under both a closed-world reading (negation as failure) and an open-world reading (Unknown allowed). Proof correctness falls with reasoning depth more than answer accuracy does.
numbers: Over 20,192 test questions: answer accuracy 99.3% (All-At-Once) and 99.2% (Iterative); proof correctness 87.1% (PRover) vs 96.2% (ProofWriter, +9 points). Birds1 test 95-100%; harder Electricity sets 80-97%. Closed-world and open-world variants both reach about 99.5-99.9% answer accuracy over all depths.
limits: Synthetic data and in-distribution. The table layout in the PDF text makes some column assignments approximate. Later work (c03, c07) shows rule-following degrades once rules truly conflict.
agent_relevance: Exceptions are handled well when the rule base is complete and stratified. Treat this as the easy case; an agent's lessons will not be stratified. Also: which assumption holds (silence means false, or unknown) must be stated in the prompt.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: A Dataset for Natural Language Reasoning with Contradictory Information
finding: Defeasible reasoning with preferences over rules, conflicting sources, and missing world knowledge. Tested fine-tuned BERT and T5, prompt-tuned PaLM 62B, and few-shot PaLM 62B, PaLM 540B and FLAN-PaLM 540B with chain-of-thought.
numbers: Three labels, majority baseline 33%. Each variant: 1000 train, 500 validation, 1000 test. Tuned models do reasonably at depth 1 but degrade at depths 2-3; few-shot models are poor at every depth, including instruction-tuned FLAN-PaLM; PaLM 540B better than 62B. Accuracy falls monotonically as conflict probability rises (0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8); BERT is near random at medium and high conflict. Type-2 conflicts (must show the overriding rule's premise cannot be proven) are harder than Type-1. Few-shot models are weak on proof quality: conflict-resolution F1 low until tuned.
quote: preference understanding and defeasible reasoning capacities do not surface out-of-the-box in pretrained LMs
limits: Per-cell scores are only in figures, so only trends and design numbers are recorded. PaLM-era models (2022-23).
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'which rule wins' being hard for models. Preference or recency ordering should be given as an explicit ranked list, or resolved by code, with the model only reading the verdict.

source: Rudinger et al. (2020) Thinking Like a Skeptic: Defeasible Inference in Natural Language (delta-NLI)
finding: Defeasible NLI: given a premise, hypothesis and an update sentence, decide whether the update strengthens or weakens the hypothesis, or generate such updates. Built on SNLI, ATOMIC and Social-Chem-101.
numbers: Classification accuracy with full input: RoBERTa 81.6 (SNLI), 78.3 (ATOMIC), 86.2 (Social) vs human 83.6, 78.2, 87.6 and majority about 50. Update-only input already gets 65.1, 65.2, 71.6. Generation is much harder: a model writes a correct weakener or strengthener up to 68% of the time (GPT2-XL). Weakeners are harder than strengtheners; the gap is 17 points for GPT2-XL and 34 for Bart. Annotator Krippendorff alpha 0.62, 0.67, 0.69.
limits: Part of the classification success is annotation artifacts (update-only baseline well above chance). Pre-2022 models.
agent_relevance: Recognising that a given update weakens a claim is nearly human-level; producing a good counter-consideration is hard. The agent should test a conclusion against concrete observed updates, not ask the model to invent exceptions on a schedule.

source: Madaan et al. (2021) Think about it! Improving defeasible reasoning by first modeling the question scenario (CURIOUS)
finding: A model first generates an inference graph of influences around the question, then uses it as extra input when judging the update. New state of the art on all three delta-NLI sets.
numbers: Accuracy delta-ATOMIC 80.2 (previous best 78.3, end-to-end without graph 78.8); delta-SNLI 85.6 (81.6; 82.2); delta-Social 88.6 (86.2; 86.7). Gains marked statistically significant. About 4 points on delta-SNLI.
limits: Fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence model, not a prompted LLM. Gains of 1.9 to 4 points.
agent_relevance: Modelling the situation before judging the update gives a few points. Supports a restate step before Revise, but the effect is small.

source: Allaway et al. (2023) Penguins Don't Fly: Reasoning about Generics through Instantiations and Exceptions
finding: Generates exemplars (instantiations where a generic holds, exceptions where it fails) for 650 generics using linguistically guided constrained decoding, and compares with few-shot GPT-3. Also shows that NLI models label generic-exception pairs inconsistently.
numbers: 19k exemplars: 12,562 instantiations and 6,297 exceptions. Precision@1 for exceptions 0.632 (ours) vs 0.517 (GPT-3); instantiations 0.911 vs 0.758. Filtering exceptions to those an NLI model labels 'contradiction' raised exception precision@1 to 0.839 (+20.7 points). Valid generations: 13.4-21.0% with beam search vs 21.0-35.7% with constrained decoding.
limits: Human-judged on samples. The authors argue NLI labels (entailment, neutral, contradiction) cannot represent default inheritance: 'penguins cannot fly' is judged neutral or contradiction inconsistently.
agent_relevance: Exceptions are the scarce data; knowledge bases rarely list them. A lesson store of defaults should record the exceptions actually seen, because the model cannot reliably generate them from nothing.

source: Leidinger, van Rooij, Shutova (2024) Are LLMs classical or nonmonotonic reasoners? Lessons from generics
finding: Seven open-weight LLMs (Llama-2-13b, Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B, OpenHermes-2.5, Starling-13B, WizardLM, Zephyr) were asked whether they believe a generic ('Birds fly'), then re-asked after an exception ('Penguins don't fly'), a supporting instance ('Owls fly'), or an irrelevant exemplar. Datasets: GEN-comm (commonsense) and GEN-abs (abstract).
numbers: Exceptions lowered agreement for all models on both datasets (p=0.01), to 0% on GEN-abs for Llama-2, Mixtral, Starling and WizardLM, as a nonmonotonic reasoner would. But supporting instances should leave agreement at 100%: on GEN-abs only Mistral, OpenHermes and WizardLM stayed above 90%, and Mixtral fell below 10%. Irrelevant random exemplars pushed agreement below 50% (GEN-comm: Llama-2, Mistral, Mixtral, Zephyr) and below 20% (GEN-abs: Llama-2, Mixtral, Starling, WizardLM, Zephyr). Only OpenHermes (code-trained) stayed above 85% on both. An alternative template and chain-of-thought gave similar results, except Llama-2 under CoT.
quote: fail to maintain stable beliefs on truth conditions of generics at the addition of supporting examples
limits: Medium-size open models, not frontier ones. Agreement is a yes/no belief probe, not a reasoning chain. The exception effect alone cannot show nonmonotonic reasoning, since the same models also move on irrelevant input.
agent_relevance: Core warning for G1: a model that doubts when shown an exception also doubts when shown noise. Code must decide which signals count as exceptions; the model should not decide whether to revise based on any added text.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench: Towards Systematic Evaluation of Logical Reasoning Ability of LLMs
finding: 25 single-step inference rules across propositional, first-order and non-monotonic logic. The non-monotonic part follows Lifschitz (1989): default reasoning with irrelevant information (DRI), several defaults (DRS), a disabled default (DRD), open domain (DRO), unknown expectations (RE1-3) and priorities (RAP). Models: Llama-2, Mistral, Gemini-Pro, ChatGPT, GPT-4, with chain-of-thought.
numbers: Yes/No-question non-monotonic averages, A(Yes)/A(No): Llama-2 57.8/43.7, Mistral 71.0/67.5, Gemini 67.8/69.7, ChatGPT 61.5/65.5, GPT-4 74.4/84.8. Multiple-choice non-monotonic averages: Llama-2 44.0, Mistral 36.5, Gemini 54.8, ChatGPT 58.8, GPT-4 69.0 (GPT-4 about 91.5 on the other logic type in the matching table). Weakest rules were several defaults (DRS; GPT-4 55.0 on MCQA) and open domain (DRO; GPT-4 45.0 on MCQA). Humans scored above 85% on yes/no (153 items, three raters, agreement 0.785).
limits: Templated single-step items. The PDF text merges several table columns, so only the non-monotonic averages above are recorded with confidence.
agent_relevance: Even GPT-4 is far below ceiling on a one-step default with exceptions, and more worse with several defaults at once. Pass only the single triggered rule into Revise rather than the whole lesson list.

source: Cooper, Sadhu, Velasquez (2026) DeFAb: A Dataset for Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
finding: Models fill gaps or propose exceptions to rules in Gene Ontology based theories; a symbolic verifier checks the consequences of each edit. Revision tasks require withdrawing the challenged prediction and keeping the others. Format of the answer changed success more than reasoning did.
numbers: 336 held-out tasks; simple symbolic repair solves all 336. Successes direct/structured prompt: GPT-5.6 Sol 336/336; GPT-6.1 Sol 336/336; Claude Sonnet 5 306/244; Claude Sonnet 5.5 133/336; DeepSeek-V4-Pro 273/38; Kimi-K2.6 205/99. Of 1,054 failures across the six models and two styles, 652 were response-contract violations, 366 hit the token limit and 36 were admissible answers that missed the semantic target. No lost protected predictions among admissible revisions.
limits: Version 2 preprint dated 23 Oct 2026, not peer reviewed. The panel is solvable by entity-local exceptions, so success does not show the model chose a good exception scope. Planned training and feedback studies had not been run.
agent_relevance: The same model went from 133 to 336 of 336 with a different prompt style. Revision should be a structured edit checked by code, including a scope check (what else changes), not free text.

source: Nananukul et al. (2025) LOGicalThought: Logic-Based Ontological Grounding of LLMs for High-Assurance Reasoning
finding: An LLM converts guideline text into a defeasible logic program run by the ErgoAI reasoner plus an ontology graph, and answers from that dual context. Tested on negation, implication and defeasible modes across four benchmarks (including ContractNLI, SARA, BiomedNLI).
numbers: Overall +11.84% across all LLMs vs four baselines; up to +10.2% on negation, +13.2% on implication and +5.5% on defeasible reasoning over the strongest baseline. Mistral-7B rose from 45.2 to 53.4 (+8.2) and LLaMA-8B from 44.3 to 50.4 (+6.1). Some drops: -0.8 on ContractNLI (defeasible), -3.2 on SARA (negation), -0.7 on BiomedNLI (negation).
limits: Defeasible gains are the smallest of the three modes. Depends on the LLM translating text into a correct program, which is the weak link. Small models gain most.
agent_relevance: A working LLM plus defeasible-solver loop. Evidence that exception rules executed by code help, though the defeasible gain (+5.5) is modest.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: The LLM translates the problem into a symbolic form (logic programming, FOL, CSP, SAT) and an external solver answers; solver error messages drive self-refinement. Tested on ProofWriter (open-world subset), PrOntoQA, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction and AR-LSAT.
numbers: ProofWriter accuracy Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: ChatGPT 35.50 / 49.17 / 58.33; GPT-3.5 36.16 / 48.33 / 71.45; GPT-4 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66. FOLIO GPT-4 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92. On PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beat Logic-LM (83.20).
limits: Not specifically defeasible. Failure to produce an executable formulation is the main loss.
agent_relevance: Shows the program-decides pattern (G5) works for rule reasoning. A solver gives a clean retract-on-conflict if the rules are formalised, but formalising is the hard step.

source: Yang, Ishay, Lee (2023) Coupling Large Language Models with Logic Programming for Robust and General Reasoning from Text (GPT-3+ASP)
finding: GPT-3 turns sentences into atoms; an answer set programming solver (Clingo) with hand-written knowledge modules, including inertia defaults in the Discrete Event Calculus, does the reasoning.
numbers: bAbI: GPT-3 few-shot 80.34%, CoT 86.18%, GPT-3 (davinci-003) + ASP 99.99% with 2 disagreements, both malformed questions. StepGame k=1..5: GPT-3 (davinci-002) + ASP 92.6 / 89.9 / 89.1 / 93.8 / 92.9 against few-shot (d3) 55 / 37 / 25 / 30 / 32 and CoT (d3) 61 / 45 / 30 / 35 / 35; k=6..10 about 88-92. Of 1000 StepGame predictions, 108 disagreed with labels and 107 of those were label errors (about 10.7% of labels wrong).
limits: ASP modules are hand-written per task. Gains come from the solver, not from the model learning exceptions.
agent_relevance: ASP is the working descendant of Reiter's default logic. If lessons are stored as rules with an exception clause, a small solver call can apply them deterministically.

source: Ishay, Yang, Lee (2023) Leveraging Large Language Models to Generate Answer Set Programs
finding: LLMs generate answer set programs for logic puzzles from few-shot examples; the ASP solver finds answers. The paper notes that ASP can express default reasoning and constraints.
numbers: The pipeline does not reach 100% accuracy ('While our pipeline doesn't achieve 100% accuracy'); per-puzzle figures were not extracted.
limits: Only skimmed for the claim above; no per-puzzle numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: LLM-written rule programs are checkable by running them, which fits G2 and G3.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories, HtT)
finding: Two stages. Induction: the LLM proposes rules while solving training examples, and a rule is kept if it appears often enough and leads to correct answers often enough. Deduction: the rule library is prepended and the model retrieves rules to answer test questions. Tested on relational (CLUTRR), numerical (base-16 arithmetic) and concept-learning problems.
numbers: Absolute gain of 10-30% in accuracy over CoT in most settings. Incorrect rules cause 65% of CoT errors on CLUTRR and 81% on base-16 arithmetic.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; per-table numbers not extracted. Rules are universal, not defaults with exceptions; there is no retraction beyond the frequency filter.
agent_relevance: A template for a lesson library: verify a rule by how often using it led to a correct answer before keeping it. The missing piece is exception handling, meaning retract or narrow the rule when a counterexample fires.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: The agent keeps a list of natural-language insights and edits it with four operators after comparing success and failure trajectories: ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE. A new insight starts at importance 2; upvote or edit raises it, downvote lowers it, and at 0 it is removed. This is defaults with retraction in practice.
numbers: ALFWorld task 'put': ReAct 50%, insights-only 61%, retrieval-only 73%, full ExpeL 83%. Insights-only vs retrieve-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. Cross-task, without repeats, ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%) and trails it on ALFWorld (54% at R3 vs 59%).
limits: The insight edits are decided by the LLM, not by a code-located conflict (contrast G2). Four-fold validation on small tasks. No ablation of the retraction rule alone.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to lessons as defaults: counts plus delete-at-zero is a cheap retraction rule that code can run. Add the requirement that a downvote cite a real failing output.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to review and correct its own answer lowers accuracy. With an oracle label telling it when it was wrong, accuracy rises, so the large gains of earlier self-correction papers come from the oracle.
numbers: Intrinsic correction, standard to round 2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8 (38.1 after round 1), HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0, HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 84.3 / 89.7 / 29.0 and GPT-4 97.5 / 85.5 / 59.0 on the same three. On GSM8K GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time, and when it changes, correct-to-incorrect exceeds incorrect-to-correct.
limits: The extracted table rows were reordered by the PDF layout; the oracle-row assignment to models follows table order and may be off in HotpotQA. 2023 models; HotpotQA samples are small (100).
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for G1 and G2: revise only when something outside the model flags a failure.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts
finding: Coherent, generated counter-evidence is accepted by models; entity-substitution counter-evidence is often resisted; and when both belief-consistent and conflicting evidence are shown, models prefer the consistent one (confirmation bias).
numbers: With substitution-style counter-memory, ChatGPT, GPT-4 and PaLM2 mostly stayed with the original answer; with generated coherent counter-memory models were highly receptive. In multi-source settings memorisation ratio rose, reaching 80% for GPT-4 on the most popular entities. Evidence order changed results by over 5 points for some models and over 30 points for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B. 50 stubborn cases were hand-checked.
limits: Entity facts (PopQA, StrategyQA), not rule exceptions. Closed-source versions from 2023.
agent_relevance: An LLM's belief revision has a built-in confirmation bias that grows with how well-known the claim is. Revise should show the conflicting evidence on its own, not beside the old claim, in a fixed order.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification
finding: An LLM writes supporting and attacking arguments and base scores; an argumentation framework (a non-monotonic formalism where attacks defeat arguments) computes the final strength by fixed gradual semantics. Compared against direct questioning, estimated confidence and chain-of-thought on claim verification.
numbers: Accuracy over StrategyClaim, TruthfulClaim and MedClaim with eight LLMs ranged from about 0.54 to 0.81 across methods. Chain-of-thought, direct questioning and ArgLLM with an estimated base score performed best; ArgLLM with fixed 0.5 base was usually lower. Best single cells: ArgLLM (estimated base, depth 1) 0.81, CoT 0.79.
limits: About equal to chain-of-thought, not better. The benefit is that decisions are traceable and contestable. Gradual-semantics argumentation is related to, but not identical with, Reiter-style defaults.
agent_relevance: A defeat structure computed by code over model-written arguments is competitive and auditable, at no accuracy cost, and leaves a retraction trace.

source: Jin et al. (2022) When to Make Exceptions: Exploring Language Models as Accounts of Human Moral Judgment (MoralExceptQA)
finding: A challenge set of 148 vignettes (456 questions) in which a rule (do not cut in line, do not damage property, no cannonballing) may be broken. Humans decide when exceptions are acceptable; LLMs are tested. The authors add MoralCoT, a prompt walking through the rule's purpose, parties affected and their utility.
numbers: MoralCoT 64.47 F1, +10.53 over base InstructGPT and +6.2 F1 over the best of seven other LLMs. Human yes-rates per vignette ranged from 31.67% to 88.37% (N=60-86 per item). Subquestion analysis: parties' utility description missed for 58.10% of parties; 38.51% of mentioned parties missed.
limits: Single benchmark with small N per item. F1 of 64 is far from ceiling.
agent_relevance: Deciding when a rule yields to an exception takes structured sub-questions (purpose, who is affected). Fits asking what the rule is for before accepting an exception.

source: Jhang (2026) Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
finding: Uses delta-SNLI items with one strengthener and one weakener each; models give a prior and posteriors in separate calls; the measure s is the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction. Varies stated vs reported ('Someone said that') evidence and one vs five weighted estimates, in seven configurations.
numbers: Stated, direct elicitation: all seven configurations move in the annotated direction, s = 18-28 percentage points. Reporting lowers s in all seven (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements. Five weighted estimates cut s by 43% and 68% in the two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) but changed it by only -3.7 to +0.5 points in the five harnessed configurations (120 pairs).
limits: Preprint, plan not publicly registered. Delta-NLI annotates only direction, so no claim about how large an update should be.
agent_relevance: Models update in the right direction on a single update but shrink the update when the evidence is hearsay. Revise should log the source type of each signal.

source: Han et al. (2024) inductive and nonmonotonic reasoning tests of LLMs (as cited in Leidinger 2024)
finding: Cited by Leidinger et al.: nonmonotonic reasoning poses a greater challenge for LLMs than other reasoning tasks, and only GPT-4 performs adequately.
numbers: No numbers read; second-hand statement only.
limits: Not opened. Not independent evidence until the original is read.
agent_relevance: Corroborates c07 and c08 but is not yet checked.

source: Elio and Pelletier (1996) and Pelletier and Elio (2005) human judgments in default inheritance (as cited in Allaway 2023)
finding: Cited by Allaway et al.: what people perceive as the correct answer in default inheritance puzzles depends on whether exemplars of the generic are present in the evidence, contrary to what the formal systems predict.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; the human side belongs to the parallel angle documents.
agent_relevance: People do not follow a single formal default logic. Use the logic as a design target for code, not as a description of human judgment.

source: Reiter (1980) A logic for default reasoning; McCarthy (1980, 1986) circumscription and abnormality predicates
finding: Founding formalisms. Reiter: a default rule says that if A holds and it is consistent to assume B, then conclude B. McCarthy: minimise the extension of an abnormality predicate. Descendants in use today include answer set programming (Clingo, DLV) and ErgoAI, as seen in c10 and c12.
numbers: Not read this session. The Sergot birds rulebase in c01, written in McCarthy-style abnormality form, is solved near-perfectly by trained transformers.
limits: Not opened. Complexity claims from memory (default reasoning is hard, on the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) are unchecked.
agent_relevance: Prefer the abnormality-predicate form (c01, c10, c12) because it is ordinary rules a program can check.

source: Kazemi et al. (2024) and Xie et al. (2023) as cited in Leidinger (2024): models struggle with contradictory information
finding: Leidinger's related work states that LLMs struggle to reason with contradictory information (Kazemi et al.) and that evidence on sensitivity to contradiction is mixed, with a confirmation bias under diverse viewpoints (Xie et al.).
numbers: None beyond c03 and c17.
limits: Secondary citation; both confirmed first-hand in c03 and c17.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the first-hand results.

source: Shi et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2023) as cited in Leidinger (2024): irrelevant input destabilises answers
finding: Irrelevant information confounds arithmetic reasoning (Shi et al.); OpenAI models fail to keep stable responses when given irrelevant objections (Wang et al.).
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: Matches c07: any added text can move a model's belief, so the trigger for revising must be checked by code.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench, conclusions on why non-monotonic items are hard
finding: The authors report that models struggle with longer rules, with negated premises, and with several defaults in one context; sometimes they overlook context or hallucinate information. They also argue that non-monotonic patterns are common in the natural text models are pre-trained on, which may explain why models do better on non-monotonic yes/no items than on propositional ones.
numbers: GPT-4 propositional modus tollens yes-accuracy dropped to about 59% while simple hypothetical syllogism was about 85%; humans above 85% on yes/no across logic types; non-monotonic multiple choice remained a challenge for both humans and LLMs.
limits: Authors' interpretation, not tested causally.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping each Revise call to one rule and one failing output, with negations stated positively.

source: Sadhu, Shahad, Marino (2026) DeReLab: Probing Defeasible Reasoning and Confirmation Bias in LLMs with a Generative Benchmark
finding: Multi-turn belief-updating dialogues with formally verified answers. Models accept evidence that supports their belief but fail to retract when evidence defeats it. Default reasoning is harder than inheritance.
numbers: 9 models; 9,029-11,682 labeled turns per model. 17 of 19 model-by-type cells show significant confirmation-bias gap (Holm-corrected). GPT-5.1 default gap 0.935, accuracy on defeating updates 3.5% (odds ratio 891). Gemma-4-12B gap 0.082. Llama-3.1-8B changes its answer wrongly on 36% of irrelevant off-path turns.
limits: Synthetic graph dialogues. Prior belief is the model's own earlier answer. One cell (Gemma-4-MoE) was a question-order artifact.
agent_relevance: Core risk for Revise (S5): a model that holds a conclusion rarely retracts on a defeater. Retraction needs an explicit mechanism, not just 'be open to new evidence'. Also guard against revising on irrelevant updates.

source: Sadhu et al. (2026) DeReLab: metacognitive dissociation and thinking scaffold
finding: Models often label an update as weakening yet still answer 'yes' to the entailment question on the same turn (know-but-don't-output). Reversing question order cut the effect-labeling score sharply. Extended thinking nearly removed the bias in Qwen3-32B.
numbers: GPT-5-mini: labels weakening 95.4% of turns but entailment accuracy 20.3%. Llama-3.1-70B: 85.1% vs 14.9%. Reversed order: Gemma-4-31B effect score 0.970 to 0.264; Qwen3-32B bias gap 0.670 to 0.816. Qwen3-32B thinking default gap 0.008 vs non-thinking 0.670. Llama-3.1-70B mislabels already-defeated chains as weakening 83.9% (semantic override by negative wording).
limits: Single benchmark family, 8 to 9 models, synthetic entities.
agent_relevance: Ask the agent to first name the effect of new evidence, then force the conclusion to be recomputed from that label as a separate step. Reasoning mode matters more than prompt wording. Negative wording alone is not a defeater.

source: Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models (2025)
finding: 28 LLMs tested on 20 default-reasoning patterns (21 with a negative variant). Top models are strong zero-shot, but chain of thought often hurts, and models blur defeasible and deductive readings of generics.
numbers: 15 uncontroversial patterns, zero-shot, temp 0: Claude 3 Opus 96.51%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96.01%, GPT-4 93.52%, Gemma 2 9B 92.69%; second tier 78-89%; 7 models near chance, 3 below chance. CoT: mean change -11.14% (SD 15.74) among models above 75%; GPT-4 -12.62, Claude 3 Sonnet -16.28, GPT-4o +17.44. Few-shot Claude 3 Opus -6.81. Premise order: Code Llama 13B 0% to about 80% on one pattern. Wording-correlation across rewordings from 0.99 to -0.05.
quote: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting often leads to serious performance degradation
limits: 20 instances per pattern. Page text read to 100,000 of 115,621 characters. Handcrafted plus generated items.
agent_relevance: Do not assume step-by-step prompting helps default reasoning. Test wording and premise order, because results are fragile. Keep exceptions stated explicitly rather than as generics.

source: Ishay and Lee (2026) LLMs as ASP Programmers: Self-Correction Enables Task-Agnostic Nonmonotonic Reasoning
finding: LLM writes Answer Set Programs (default negation, exceptions) and a solver gives feedback for iterative repair. Large gains on nonmonotonic tasks over plain LLMs and over SMT-based coupling. Self-correction is the main driver.
numbers: Average over 6 benchmarks: 78.0% vs 51.3% baseline (+52% relative); 54.6% without revisions to 78.0% with. MultiLogicNMR skeptical 90.5% vs 59.0%, credulous 81.0% vs 52.9% (Gemini 2.5 Pro+ASP 100% skeptical). LLM+SMT only 35.8% / 35.0% (chance 33.3%). BoardgameQA 82.4% vs 84.7% baseline: no gain overall. ZL-XXL 71.3% vs 24.2%. Non-reasoning DeepSeek V3 only 45.0%. Compact reference guide 70.0% vs 61.4% with none.
quote: stable model semantics allow LLMs to naturally express default rules and exceptions
limits: Needs strong reasoning models. Verbose documentation hurts ('context rot'). Syntax errors dominate first attempts (360 vs 18 after revisions).
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that default rules plus exceptions are expressible by an LLM and checkable by code with retry on solver errors. A retract-on-conflict rule can be run by a solver, not by the model's judgment.

source: Tachmazidis, Batsakis, Antoniou (2024) Benchmarking Defeasible Reasoning with LLMs - Initial Experiments and Future Directions
finding: Defeasible-logic reasoner benchmark theories (chains, circles, DAGs, hierarchies) translated to text with invented predicate names. GPT-4o inference compared with defeasible-logic conclusions.
numbers: No aggregate accuracy reported; case-by-case tables over 8 theory types via chat links.
limits: Preliminary, qualitative, single model. Found mismatch with priority rules; the model sometimes worked backwards from the chain start and did not follow defeasible semantics.
agent_relevance: Priority between conflicting rules (which exception wins) is where a plain LLM drifts from the formal answer. Encode priority explicitly.
